# Preface {.unnumbered}

Welcome to MATH7432, *Computing and Algorithms for Statistics* — a Master's module at
Lancaster University about the computational machinery that makes modern statistics run.
Statistics on paper is elegant; statistics in practice is code. This module teaches you to
write that code well, and to understand the algorithms it implements. Everything is in
both R and Python.

A word on the two languages before anything else. Every code chunk in these notes appears
twice, side by side: **R on the left, Python on the right**, translated line for line. You
are expected to **learn one language, not both** — pick whichever you prefer, unless your
programme dictates the choice — and follow its column through the notes. The other column
is not extra homework; it is a bridge. Sooner or later every working statistician has to
cross from one language to the other, and when your turn comes these notes double as a
phrasebook. One practical consequence: the side-by-side layout needs horizontal room, so
read the notes on a wide screen — they were not designed for phones.

## Where we are going {.unnumbered}

The module has a deliberate arc, so here it is up front:

- **Weeks 1–4 — Programming in R and Python** (each week: 1h lecture + 2h lab). We start
  from zero and build up the language: variables, vectors and matrices (@sec-week1); logic, loops
  and iteration (@sec-week2); functions and functional programming (@sec-week3); data
  frames and plotting (@sec-week4). A single running example threads through these weeks:
  **gradient descent**, the workhorse optimiser behind half of modern statistics and
  essentially all of machine learning. It appears in week 2 as a humble loop and grows up
  alongside your programming skills.

- **Week 5 — Optimisation for statistics** (2h lecture + 1h lab). The payoff chapter,
  where the programming tools meet the statistics: estimation as loss minimisation,
  stochastic gradient descent, momentum, preconditioning, and quasi-Newton methods
  (BFGS) — see @sec-week5.

- **Weeks 6–7 — The bootstrap.** Nonparametric, parametric and semi-parametric
  bootstraps; standard errors, confidence intervals, and bias correction. Week 6 also
  hosts the **in-class test**.

- **Weeks 8–10 — Markov chain Monte Carlo.** Random-walk Metropolis,
  Metropolis–Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, convergence diagnostics, and Gibbs
  sampling.

**These notes cover weeks 1–5**, plus a bonus chapter on classes and multiple
dispatch, in both languages (@sec-bonus), for the curious — optional self-study, no
timetabled slot. The
materials for weeks 6–10 will be released separately later in term.

## How to use these notes {.unnumbered}

These notes are meant to be *used*, not read like a novel. The intended workflow:

- **Before the lecture:** skim the week's chapter. You don't need to understand
  everything — the lecture will give you the overview and the why.
- **In the lab:** work through the chapter at your own pace, copy-pasting the code into
  RStudio and running it yourself. Change things. Break things. Fix them. Exercises
  appear throughout each chapter exactly where the relevant idea is fresh — do them as
  you meet them, not in a guilty batch the night before the test.
- **Afterwards:** worked solutions are released on Moodle once all of the week's labs
  have ended.

Code you are meant to run appears in grey boxes; its output appears just below. If your
output disagrees with ours, one of us has a bug, and the smart money is rarely on the
notes (though it does happen — tell us when it does).

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

An honest word on what we assume. **Mathematical maturity: yes.** You are Master's
students; we will use calculus and linear algebra notation — gradients, matrices,
eigenvalues — without apology. **Programming background: none.** If you have never
written a line of code in your life, you are exactly who week 1 was written for. It
starts from zero; it just doesn't linger there. If you *have* programmed before, the
early weeks will be quick revision with the occasional language-specific surprise.

## Sources {.unnumbered}

These notes build on, and reuse material from, two earlier Lancaster modules:

- Gaetano Romano and Eduard Campillo-Funollet, *MATH245 Computational Mathematics*,
  Lancaster University — also the source of the side-by-side R/Python format. MATH245
  itself descends from the lineage of Debbie Costain, Clement Lee, Chris Nemeth, Tom
  Palmer, Florian Pein, Gaetano Romano and Stuart Sharples.
- *MATH550/SCC.461 R Programming* (Statistics in Practice / Programming for Data
  Scientists), Lancaster University,
  <https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/~romano/teaching/2324MATH550/>.

For going deeper into R than we do here, the canonical further reading is
Hadley Wickham, *Advanced R*, 2nd edition, <https://adv-r.hadley.nz/> — free online, and
the source of several ideas and examples in these notes.

Right then. Open RStudio — or your Python editor of choice — and let's begin with
@sec-week1.
